say: You give it an inequality in $n$ and a starting value. It **proves** the inequality holds for every $n$ from that value on.
The key idea: show it is true for the first value, then show that if it is true for $n = k$ it must be true for $n = k+1$. The first value starts the chain and the step keeps it going.

how.higher: Higher level only. It has come up as a 15-mark part of its own on Paper 1 (2019 Q2(b): prove $3^n \ge 4n+1$ for $n \ge 2$).

example.question: Prove by induction that $2^n > 2n$ for all $n \ge 3$, $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

steps.title: Test the first value
steps.say: Check the statement for the starting value $n = 3$.

steps.title: Assume it for k
steps.say: Assume the statement is true for $n = k$, where $k \ge 3$. This is the fact you will use.

steps.title: State what to prove
steps.say: Write what $P(k+1)$ says. This is the target.

steps.title: Use the assumption
steps.say: Multiply both sides of $\hl{1}{2^k > 2k}$ by $2$. Then show $4k$ is at least $2k + 2$.

steps.title: Write the conclusion
steps.say: State what you have shown. This line carries a mark.

lines.text: If true for $n = k$, then true for $n = k+1$. It is true for $n = 3$. Hence it is true for all $n \ge 3$, $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

higher.tip: Write all three statements: the start value, $P(k)$ and $P(k+1)$. Each earns marks, and the order does not matter.
Missing one of the three statements costs marks quickly, so write each one out, even when it looks obvious.
The key step is using $P(k)$ to prove $P(k+1)$. Show that line clearly.
Finish with a conclusion. Leaving it out loses a mark.

say: You start by assuming $\sqrt{2} = \frac{p}{q}$ in lowest terms. The method shows this assumption **contradicts** itself, so $\sqrt{2}$ cannot be rational.
The key idea: squaring gives $p^2 = 2q^2$, which forces $p$ and then $q$ to be even. Two even numbers share a factor $2$, and that breaks "lowest terms".

how.higher: Higher level only. It has been a 10-mark part of its own on Paper 1 twice: 2019 Q6(b) and 2023 Q3(a).

steps.title: Assume the opposite
steps.say: Assume $\sqrt{3}$ is rational. Then it is a fraction in lowest terms, with $a$ and $b$ whole numbers that have no common factor.

steps.title: Square both sides
steps.say: Square both sides and clear the fraction.

lines.text: So $a^2$ is a multiple of $3$. Since $3$ is prime, $\hl{1}{a}$ is a multiple of $3$.
So $b^2$ is a multiple of $3$, and so $\hl{2}{b}$ is a multiple of $3$.

steps.title: State the contradiction
steps.say: Both $a$ and $b$ are multiples of $3$, so they have a common factor $3$.

lines.text: This contradicts HCF$(a, b) = 1$. So the assumption was false, and $\sqrt{3}$ is irrational.

higher.tip: Begin with the assumption, and say the fraction is in lowest terms. The contradiction later depends on it.

sources.quote: where p and q have no common factors (simplest form)

higher.tip: Marks are given for showing the first number is even, then the second. Write each step, even if the rest goes wrong.

sources.quote: deduces that p is even or equivalent

higher.tip: Show $q$ is even too, by writing it as $2m$ or an equivalent form.
End by saying the common factor contradicts the assumption. Do not stop at "both are even".

say: You give it a function $f(x)$. It finds a function $F(x)$ whose **derivative** is $f(x)$, then adds $+c$.
The key idea: integrating undoes differentiating. Ask which expression you would differentiate to get $f(x)$, and check by differentiating your answer.

steps.title: Try a power of x
steps.say: The answer must differentiate to $8x^3$. Differentiating gives a power one lower, so try $x^4$.

lines.text: This is close, but we need $8x^3$, which is twice as big.

steps.title: Fix the number
steps.say: Multiply by $2$ to double the result.

steps.title: Add the constant
steps.say: A constant disappears when you differentiate, so $2x^4 + 5$ also works, and so does $2x^4 - 7$. Add $\hl{1}{c}$ to cover all of them.

say: You give it a sum of terms $kx^a$. It integrates each term and adds $+c$.
The key idea: for each term, **add 1** to the power, then **divide** by the new power. Turn roots and fractions into powers first.

how.higher: Higher level asks it directly as a 5-mark part on Paper 1 (2019 Q4(a), 2022 Q2(a)). It is also the first step inside definite integrals, areas between curves and average-value questions.

steps.title: Write roots as powers
steps.say: A root has to become a power before you can integrate it.

steps.title: Integrate each term
steps.say: For each term, add $1$ to the power and divide by the new power.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.say: Join the terms with their signs. Add $\hl{1}{c}$ once, at the end.

higher.tip: Always add $+c$ to an indefinite integral. Leaving it out costs a mark.
Each term you integrate correctly earns credit. Work through every term, as each is a marked step.
Even an incomplete attempt earns partial credit if some integration is correct, so write the integral down.
For a definite integral, show the integration. Without it you get no credit at all.

sources.quote: Indication of integration is required to be awarded any credit
